name: business-delegate
intent: Preserve a stable, coarse-grained client-facing contract over a remote business service by hiding lookup, transport and infrastructure failures (Core J2EE Patterns, presentation tier). Because dependency injection and generated clients have absorbed the lookup-hiding role, in modern systems the delegate earns its place only by owning domain mapping, batching or remote-call policy—not by renaming a generated stub.
problem: Presentation-tier code that invokes a remote business API directly must know JNDI or service discovery, generated-client or transport types, wire errors and retry/deadline rules; it becomes chatty and brittle when the endpoint or protocol changes. Conversely, inserting a delegate where DI or codegen has already erased the lookup adds ceremony, hides latency and drifts as a second API surface, so the layer must be justified by batching, policy or a stable domain-facing contract.
context: Use at a real process or network boundary where a client invokes a remote business service—classically EJB/JNDI and RMI-IIOP, now commonly REST/HTTP, gRPC or a vendor SDK—and several callers need the same endpoint, policy or semantic mapping. The remote API is more volatile or infrastructure-heavy than the client's needs, while lookup/configuration, deadlines, credential propagation, exception translation, bounded caching or retries need one owner without moving business rules into the client.
benefits: Decoupling: the presentation tier no longer knows how services are named, located or reached; service API changes are absorbed in one component.
Exception translation: infrastructure and transport exceptions become application-level errors, giving every caller one uniform failure contract.
Caching of service references and results removes repeated lookups and cuts network round trips (the Core J2EE 'Impacts Performance' consequence).
One carrier for cross-cutting remote concerns: retry/failover, authentication context propagation, metrics and logging are implemented once.
Testability and substitution: clients depend on a local interface, so a stub can stand in for the delegate without touching call sites.
Multiple client types (web, thick, mobile) share one delegate and therefore one service access policy.
Boundary clarity: callers get a coarse-grained contract and an explicit remote-failure model instead of accidentally treating a network hop as an in-process call.
tradeoffs: The delegate duplicates the remote API surface: every service operation must be declared and maintained on the delegate as well.
It hides remoteness, so developers treat calls as local and issue chatty fine-grained requests, multiplying round trips; Oracle names this explicitly as the pattern's own trap.

Cached references and handles go stale - after failover, redeploy or session expiry a cached handle points at a dead target, turning transient faults into persistent ones without a lifetime and re-lookup policy.
Exception translation can destroy diagnostics: mapping a RemoteException/HttpRequestException to an application error without chaining the cause hides retryable from fatal failures.
Caching lookup state invites concurrency bugs; synchronizing the whole delegate serializes client calls, leaving the cache unsynchronized races.
Automatic retry/recovery inside the delegate can duplicate non-idempotent operations and mask a systemic outage from the caller.
It can grow into a god object over the business tier: a one-to-one mirror of every remote service is a parallel API, not an abstraction.

participants.responsibility: Presentation-tier component (page controller, view, view helper, mobile screen) that needs business operations and calls them through the delegate instead of touching the remote API.

Client-side abstraction that exposes only the operations the client needs; obtains the service through the lookup service, caches references/results, translates infrastructure exceptions into application exceptions and may apply retry or recovery policy.
Encapsulates naming and discovery details (JNDI, service discovery, registry, base-URL configuration) and may cache service handles; typically realized as a Service Locator or the DI container.
Remote business-tier component (session bean, session facade, microservice endpoint) that performs the requested operation; located and invoked only through the delegate.

use_cases: A web or thick-client presentation tier calling EJB/remote session beans through a delegate that hides JNDI lookup and RMI-IIOP transport.
A BFF or SSR layer talking to several backend microservices through per-service delegates that centralize auth headers, timeouts, retry and error mapping.
A mobile application in front of a media or payment API where the delegate caches service handles and translates HTTP failures into user-facing states.
Introducing a seam before a migration: a delegate in front of a still-local business API so the later switch to HTTP/gRPC does not touch client code.
B2B integration where the delegate also adapts legacy or XML payloads (the Core J2EE 'Delegate Adapter' strategy) on the way to the remote service.
Microservice frontend (BFF pattern) aggregating calls to multiple downstream services behind a unified delegate surface, reducing client-specific logic in the presentation tier.
Thick-client desktop or rich mobile app consuming a backend platform API where network instability is common and the delegate provides offline-friendly retry with explicit back-off.
A Spring application using HTTP Service Clients and HttpServiceProxyFactory as an injected proxy, with a hand-written delegate only where DTO/domain mapping, batching or policy is needed.
.NET service code using IHttpClientFactory typed clients to centralize endpoint configuration, outgoing handlers, resilience and application-level error mapping behind an injected interface.
A gRPC C++ client generated from a .proto contract, wrapped by a domain-facing class that sets per-call deadlines and translates grpc::Status instead of exposing generated transport types.

SoundCloud's Backends for Frontends: client-specific BFF services (Mobile API, Web API, partner APIs) acting as delegate gateways in front of extracted microservices and the legacy monolith, centralizing auth, rate limiting and payload shaping per frontend.

Strangler-style migration where the delegate in front of legacy endpoints is progressively rewired to new services without touching presentation code — the BFF proxy initially forwarded to the monolith, then to each extracted microservice.
A Spring Security OAuth2 setup where HTTP service clients annotated with @ClientRegistrationId carry the credential and transport policy, so callers see only business operations.
avoid_when: Client and service live in the same process with no lookup or transport to hide: a plain interface or function call is the whole answer.

A framework already generates the client proxy from the contract (gRPC stub, Feign, Retrofit, OpenAPI codegen) and no translation/caching policy is added: the delegate would only rename the generated client.
There is a single call site and no anticipated change of transport: a private wrapper function is simpler than a delegate component.
The remote contract is stable, close to the local model, and no caching, retry or error translation is required (plain Gateway plus DTOs suffices).
The 'remote' hop is a local in-process library behind a stable interface: the indirection buys nothing.
A DI container already injects a typed or generated client and callers need no domain mapping or additional policy: adding another delegate only recreates EJB-era lookup ceremony.

The proposed delegate would make a remote interface look local without coarse-grained operations, explicit deadlines, cancellation and failure semantics: fix the remote contract or keep the transport boundary visible.
anti_patterns: Mirror every remote method -> the delegate becomes a parallel API that must track every service change -> publish a client-shaped, coarse-grained subset instead.
Pretend delegate calls are local -> callers issue chatty fine-grained requests and multiply latency -> document remoteness and batch operations behind the boundary.

Put business rules, orchestration or transactions in the delegate -> policy is duplicated outside the business tier and becomes a distributed transaction script -> keep the delegate to access, translation and remote-call policy.
Cache remote handles forever -> failover or redeploy turns a transient fault into a persistent one -> use bounded lifetimes and stale-handle re-resolution.
Drop the transport cause when translating errors -> operators lose the diagnostic and retryability signal -> chain the cause and retain status or error classification.
Synchronize the whole delegate to protect a cache -> unrelated calls serialize and throughput collapses -> guard only cache initialization and use a concurrent cache.
Let the delegate absorb Session Facade responsibilities -> one client-side object becomes a multi-service god object -> put cross-service workflow in a server-side facade or application service.
Cache results without TTL, invalidation or tenant keys -> callers receive stale or cross-tenant data -> bound the cache and key it by authorization and request semantics.

Expose generated transport DTOs and exceptions -> presentation code becomes coupled to the client library and wire schema -> map at the delegate boundary while preserving the cause and relevant status.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: transport and lookup mechanics vs. presentation logic.
Dependency inversion: clients depend on a local interface, not on the remote API or transport.
Information hiding / least knowledge: naming, protocol and endpoint details never leave the delegate and its lookup collaborator.
Single responsibility: lookup, invocation, error translation and retry policy each have an owner inside the delegate layer.
Open/closed: swap the transport, endpoint or service version behind the same client-facing interface without touching call sites.
best_practices: Expose a client-facing interface and inject it, so tests can substitute a stub and call sites never import the transport.
Keep the delegate thin: lookup, invocation, translation, policy — no business rules.
Always chain the original transport exception when translating, and preserve retryable-vs-fatal information.
Give cached handles and cached results an explicit lifetime, an invalidation trigger and a re-lookup path on stale-handle failures.
Protect the handle cache with a concurrent structure or a narrow lock; never synchronize the whole delegate.
Aggregate or batch remote operations behind coarse delegate methods so the hidden transport does not become chatty.
Pair one delegate with one remote conversation (typically one-to-one with a Session Facade) instead of one delegate over many services; push multi-service aggregation into the Session Facade.
Apply retry/failover only to idempotent operations, and surface exhaustion as an application error.
Keep the Lookup Service as a separate component (e.g., Service Locator pattern) rather than embedding lookup logic directly in the delegate, so lookup strategy can evolve independently.
Prefer Delegate Adapter strategy for B2B or heterogeneous integration (XML payloads, protocol translation); prefer Delegate Proxy for homogeneous service calls.
Document the remote characteristics of the delegate clearly for all consumers — avoid implicit remoteness that leads to chatty call patterns.
Use a circuit breaker inside the delegate for non-idempotent operations to prevent cascading failures when the downstream service is degraded.
Treat generated clients as transport components: add a delegate only for domain mapping, batching, auth context or resilience that callers should not duplicate.
Make deadlines, cancellation and retry idempotency part of the delegate contract; do not hide unbounded waits behind a local-looking method.
sources: Alur, Crupi & Malks, Core J2EE Patterns: Best Practices and Design Strategies, 2nd ed. (2003) — Business Delegate (Presentation Tier Patterns).
Deepak Alur, John Crupi & Dan Malks, J2EE Design Patterns (O'Reilly, 2003) — Business Delegate chapter.

related_patterns_notes.service-locator: resolves naming or discovery; keep it behind the delegate rather than making every client perform lookup.
related_patterns_notes.session-facade: aggregates business workflow on the server; the delegate stays a client-side access and policy boundary and usually pairs one-to-one with it.
related_patterns_notes.remote-facade: exposes coarse-grained remote operations; Business Delegate hides client-side access and translates failures rather than hosting server workflow.
related_patterns_notes.data-transfer-object: carries request and response data across the boundary; it is a payload shape, not the delegate's lookup or policy layer.
related_patterns_notes.service-stub: generated or provided transport client; wrap it only when a stable domain seam, batching or policy is needed.
related_patterns_notes.proxy: forwards calls through a compatible interface; Business Delegate may use proxy strategy but adds lookup, translation and client policy.
related_patterns_notes.facade: simplifies any subsystem interface; Business Delegate is a remote client-side specialization and must not absorb server business workflow.
related_patterns_notes.gateway: encapsulates access to an external resource; choose it for protocol or data-source integration, and Business Delegate when the client-facing remote business contract is the concern.
